captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 3: Cells. Have you ever wondered what you are really made of?
Today we will discover what cells are, what is inside them, how they do special jobs, and how they work together to build a living thing.
Every living thing – from the smallest bacterium to the largest whale – is built from cells.
Think of a brick wall. Each brick is a small part that builds the whole wall.
In the same way, your body is built from millions of tiny building blocks called cells.
All living things – called organisms – are made up of cells.
Plants and animals are made of many cells. They are multicellular organisms. We are multicellular too.
Some organisms are only one single cell. They are unicellular organisms, such as bacteria and yeast.
Organisms so small that we need a microscope to see them are called microorganisms. All unicellular organisms are microorganisms.
How did scientists find out about cells? Our ideas developed step by step over many years.
Around 1021, the Muslim scholar Ibn al-Haytham explained how lenses work. Microscopes depend on lenses.
Robert Hooke looked at cork through a compound microscope. He saw tiny boxes that looked like small rooms, and called them cells.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made very good lenses that magnified about 200 times. He was able to see unicellular organisms.
In 1839, Schleiden (who studied plants) and Schwann (who studied animals) shared their findings and developed cell theory.
About 15 years later, Rudolf Virchow added a new idea: all cells come from cells that already exist.
Cell theory has three main statements.
One: all living things are made up of one or more cells.
Two: cells are the basic units of life.
Three, added by Virchow: all cells come from pre-existing cells – cells that were already there.
This shows that scientific theories can change and grow when new discoveries are made.
We use a light microscope to see cells. Let's learn its main parts.
The eyepiece is the lens we look through.
The objective lens is close to the specimen and magnifies it.
The specimen slide sits on the stage. Stage clips hold the slide still.
We turn the coarse and fine adjustment wheels to get a sharp, clear image.
The light source shines light through the specimen, and the diaphragm controls how much light reaches it.
We carry the microscope by holding the arm and the base. The base keeps it stable.
It is called a light microscope because light passes through the object we are looking at.
To look at cells, we first prepare a specimen slide.
Place a thin piece of the specimen – the object we want to observe – on a glass slide.
Add a tiny drop of liquid, such as water.
Carefully lower a thin coverslip over the specimen.
Then place the slide on the microscope stage.
Stay safe: never point a microscope mirror at the Sun, and handle coverslips carefully.
Now let's use the microscope correctly.
Always start with the lowest-power objective lens.
Bring the image into focus using the coarse adjustment wheel.
When you change to a higher-power lens, use only the fine adjustment wheel. The coarse wheel could push the lens into the slide and damage it.
Remember: cells look flat under the microscope, but they are really three-dimensional.
Total magnification = magnification of the eyepiece lens × magnification of the objective lens.
Example: an eyepiece of ×10 and an objective lens of ×15 give a total magnification of ×150.
Try this: van Leeuwenhoek's lens magnified ×200. How long would a 0.1 mm object appear? Pause and work it out.
0.1 mm × 200 = 20 mm. The object would look 20 millimetres long.

captions: This diagram is a model of a typical plant cell. Let's look at each part.
The nucleus controls all the cell's activities. It contains strands of DNA.
The cytoplasm is a jelly-like material. Materials are made and broken down in it.
The cell membrane is a thin layer around the cell. It controls what goes in and out.
Mitochondria release energy from food by chemical reactions called aerobic respiration.
The cell wall is strong and stiff, made of cellulose. It supports the cell and gives it a regular shape.
Chloroplasts contain green chlorophyll, which captures light energy so the plant can make food by photosynthesis.
The large sap vacuole is filled with cell sap. It takes in water to keep the cell firm.
You can see these parts yourself by looking at onion cells under a microscope.
Now an animal cell, for example a cell from the inside of your cheek.
Like a plant cell, it has a nucleus that controls the cell and contains DNA.
The cytoplasm fills most of the animal cell.
A thin cell membrane surrounds the cell and controls what goes in and out.
Mitochondria release energy from food by aerobic respiration.
You can observe cheek cells safely using a sterile cotton bud – only use cells from your own body.
Let's compare plant cells and animal cells.
Both have a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane and mitochondria.
Only plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large sap vacuole.
In an animal cell, the cytoplasm fills almost the whole cell. In a plant cell, the large sap vacuole takes up most of the space.
Animal cells usually have more mitochondria, because animals move much more and need more energy.
Think about it: why do plant cells need cell walls, but animal cells do not? Hint: think of tall trees.

req.prompt: Label the plant cell (model). Choose a label, then tap the matching numbered dot – or use the drop-down list.

confuse.Cell wall|Cell membrane: Wall = thick OUTER layer (cellulose). Membrane = thin layer just INSIDE the wall.
confuse.Chloroplast|Mitochondrion: Chloroplasts are green discs (photosynthesis). Mitochondria are small oval/orange structures (respiration).
confuse.Sap vacuole|Cytoplasm: The vacuole is the large central space with sap; cytoplasm is the thin jelly layer around it.
confuse.Nucleus|Chloroplast: There is ONE large nucleus; there are MANY small chloroplasts.

req.hint: A plant cell has two outer layers: a thick one (the wall) and a thin one just inside it (the membrane).
req.reason: Outer thick → wall; thin just inside → membrane; big central space → vacuole; green discs → chloroplasts; one large round → nucleus.

captions: A multicellular organism has different types of cells. Their shapes and structures let them do specific jobs. We say they are specialised.
A root hair cell has a long extension that pushes out into the soil.
This extension increases the surface area of the cell, so it can absorb water and mineral salts quickly.
A palisade cell is found near the upper surface of a leaf.
It is tall and column-shaped, with many chloroplasts. This lets it absorb a lot of light energy for photosynthesis.
Animals have specialised cells too.
Ciliated cells line our air passages. Their cilia beat together to move mucus and trapped dust away from the lungs.
Red blood cells contain haemoglobin to carry oxygen. They have no nucleus, and their dimpled disc shape gives a large surface area to take up oxygen quickly.
Nerve cells, or neurones, carry electrical impulses. Branched endings receive messages and a long fibre carries them quickly.
Amazing fact: some nerve cells are as thin as a hair but up to a metre long! When cells share out different jobs, we call it division of labour.

captions: Next, how are cells organised in a multicellular organism?
A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a function.
Plant tissues include epidermal tissue, which protects the plant, xylem, which carries water, and phloem, which carries food.
Animal tissues include muscle, nerve, fat, epithelial and bone tissue. Each one has its own job.
Different tissues group together to form organs.
An organ is made of different tissues that work together. Organs carry out important functions.
Plant organs: flowers help the plant reproduce, the stem supports it and moves water, leaves make food, and roots absorb water and anchor the plant.
Human organs include the brain, eyes, lungs, heart and stomach. Each has its own function.
Organs work together in organ systems.
Several organs working together form an organ system. Each system has a different job.
In plants, the roots, stem and leaves form the water transport system. The root system anchors the plant, and flowers are part of the reproductive system.
Humans have 11 organ systems. Here are six: skeletal, respiratory, muscular, circulatory, digestive and excretory.
Let's put it all together.
It starts with a cell, for example a muscle cell.
Similar cells form a tissue – muscle tissue.
Different tissues form an organ, such as the heart.
Organs work together in an organ system – the heart and blood vessels form the circulatory system.
All the organ systems together make the whole organism – a human being.
Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. Every level works together so the organism functions efficiently. Isn't it amazing that it all starts with a tiny cell?
